query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Laser remelting of high-entropy alloy surfaces reduces the coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined microstructure with submicron-scale basket weave
generation.mechanism: Increased Vickers microhardness, nanohardness, and strain hardening exponent, leading to improved wear resistance
generation.predicted_outcome: 23% reduction in average friction coefficient and 80% reduction in wear rate
generation.baseline: As-cast Al0.65CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without laser remelting
generation.boundary: Temperature range and laser remelting parameters
generation.uncertainty: Optimal laser remelting parameters and temperature range for maximum wear resistance

falsification_experiment.design: Reciprocating sliding friction and wear tests using a ball-type friction tester
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser remelted sample shows no significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the as-cast sample, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
The laser remelting technique was applied to the surface modification of the Al0.65CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) to further advance its mechanical potential. The microstructure of the remelted layer was refined from coarse dendritic to submicron-scale basket weave compared with the as-cast substrate, resulting in a 1.8-time increase in Vickers microhardness. The nanoindentation tests indicated that the nanohardness of the remelted layer was higher than that of each phase in the substrate. Meanwhile, the remelted layer retained considerable plasticity, as evidenced by its high Wp/Wt ratio (0.763) and strain hardening exponent (0.302). Additionally, adhesive wear prevailed on the substrate, while only abrasive wear features were observed on the remelted layer. Accordingly, the average friction coefficient and the wear rate of the remelted layer were minimized by 23% and 80%, respectively, compared with the substrate. Our findings explored an industrialized method to enhance the surface properties of the Al0.65CoCrFeNi HEA and also provided some helpful references for its laser additive manufacturing.

This technique has some inherent advantages, such as simple process, flexible operation, and economic efficiency, and is already used in conventional alloys, such as Fe [], Al [], Mg [], and Ti []. Erdogan et al. [] studied the effect of LR on the surface structure and properties of electric current assistive sintered CoCrFeNiAlxTiy HEAs.
